sections.body: The cost price (CP) is what a seller paid. The selling price (SP) is what the buyer pays. If SP is more than CP the seller makes a profit. If SP is less, there is a loss.
Profit = SP - CP. Profit percent = profit ÷ CP × 100. It is always out of the cost price, not the selling price. If CP is 40 and SP is 50, profit is 10 and the profit percent is 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25%.
To find SP from a profit percent, multiply the cost by (1 + percent/100). A 20% profit on 500 gives SP = 500 × 1.2 = 600. To go the other way and find the cost, divide: 600 ÷ 1.2 = 500.
A discount is taken off the marked price. 10% off a marked price of 500 gives 500 × 0.9 = 450. A discount is out of the marked price.
Find a real price tag. Work out the selling price after 15% off, and decide what profit percent a shop would make if its cost were 20% below the marked price.
Always ask 'out of what?'. Profit is a percent of cost, discount is a percent of the marked price. These are practice numbers, not business advice.

quiz.q: A shop buys a bag for 250 and sells it for 300. What is the profit percent?
hints: Find the profit in money first, then compare it with the cost price.
Profit = 300 - 250. Divide it by the cost (250) and multiply by 100.
Example: cost 40, sold at 50 → profit 10, and 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25%. Use the same steps.

quiz.q: A jacket is marked at 800 and sold at a 15% discount. What does the buyer pay?
hints: The buyer pays what is left after the discount.
Find 15% of 800, then subtract it. Or multiply by 0.85.
Example: marked 500 with 10% off → 500 × 0.9 = 450. Use the same idea with 800 and 15%.

quiz.q: A trader sells a clock for 600 and makes a 20% profit. What did the clock cost?
hints: The selling price is the cost plus 20% of the cost.
So SP = cost × 1.2. Divide SP by 1.2 to get the cost.
Example: sold for 750 at a 25% profit → cost = 750 ÷ 1.25 = 600. Do the same with the new numbers.
